items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the urban development corporation act, in relation to allowing
businesses to use funds received from the minority and women-owned business
development and lending program for the purpose of refinancing existing debt
items.lawSection: New York State Urban Development Corporation Act
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S2296

SPONSOR: SANDERS
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the urban development corporation act, in relation to
allowing businesses to use funds received from the minority and women-
owned business development and lending program for the purpose of refi-
nancing existing debt

 
PURPOSE:

Allows businesses to use funds received from minority and women-owned
business development and lending program for the purpose of refinancing
existing debt.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1. Subparagraphs (vi) and (vii) of paragraph (c) of subdivision
1 of section 16-c of section 1 of chapter 174 of the laws of 1968,
constituting the urban development corporation act, as added by chapter
169 of the law of 1994, are amended.

 
EXISTING LAW:

The state Minority and Women Owned Business Enterprises goals do not
currently apply to municipalities.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Currently, the minority and women-owned business development and lending
program does not allow small business to do debt refinancing.  Modifying
this existing loan program would permit a small business to refinance
existing debt on more favorable terms, which would allow these busi-
nesses to improve their cash flow. Too often, commercial credit cards
are the first and only means for small businesses to access credit. And
while credit cards provide relatively easy and convenient credit, inter-
est rates are substantially higher (often topping @20%) than loans
available through banks, credit unions, or CDFIs. For example, a small
business with $20,000 in credit card debt could expect to pay $4,000 or
more a year in interest on credit card debt. However, if the business
could refinance that debt under one of the State's existing micro-loan
programs, the interest payments could fall to as little as $1,200 to
$1,600, saving the business nearly $3,000 a year.

(www.nysmalllbiztaskforce.org)

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2011: Referred to Economic Development;

2012: Referred to Economic Development;

2013-2014: Referred to Economic Development;

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None

 
LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.

BILL NUMBER: S2296A        Revised 3/4/2020

SPONSOR: SANDERS
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the urban development corporation act, in relation to
allowing businesses to use funds received from the minority and women-
owned business development and lending program for the purpose of refi-
nancing existing debt

 
PURPOSE:

Allows businesses to use funds received from Minority and Women-Owned
Business Development and Lending Program of the Empire State Development
Corporation for the purpose of refinancing existing debt.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1. Subparagraphs (vi) and (vii) of paragraph (c) of subdivision
1 of section 16-c of section 1 of Chapter 174 of the Laws of 1968,
constituting the urban development corporation act, as added by chapter
169 of the law of 1994, are amended. A debt may be refinanced if the
chairperson of the Empire State Development Corporation finds the
original debt to be unreasonable.

 
EXISTING LAW:

The state Minority and Women Owned Business Enterprises goals do not
currently apply to municipalities.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Currently, the Minority and Women-Owned Business Development and Lending
Program does not allow small business to do debt refinancing.  Modifying
this existing loan program would permit a small business to refinance
existing debt on more favorable terms, which would allow these busi-
nesses to improve their cash flow. Too often, commercial credit cards
are the first and only means for small businesses to access credit. And
while credit cards provide relatively easy and convenient credit, inter-
est rates are substantially higher (often topping @20%) than loans
available through banks, credit unions, or CDFIs. For example, a small
business with $20,000 in credit card debt could expect to pay $4,000 or
more a year in interest on credit card debt. However, if the business
could refinance that debt under one of the State's existing micro-loan
programs, the interest payments could fall to as little as $1,200 to
$1,600, saving the business nearly $3,000 a year.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2011-12: A.8037 Referred to assembly economic development

2013-14: A.4350 Referred to assembly economic development

2015-16: 5.5737 REFERRED TO SENATE CORPORATIONS, AUTHORITIES AND COMMIS-
SIONS

2015-17: A.7719 Referred to assembly economic development


2017-18: S.3218 REFERRED TO SENATE CORPORATIONS, AUTHORITIES AND COMMIS-
SIONS

2017-18: A.491 Referred to assembly economic development

2019:S.2296-A passed Senate

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None

 
LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
